questions.prompt: DESIGN IT — [senior] funnels, retention cohorts and erasure on a cookieless analytics store (masterumami, umami/fabledocs/upskill/03-architecture-and-patterns/02-data-model-and-persistence.md). Scenario: product wants five-step funnels, weekly retention cohorts and a GDPR erasure path. The deployment serves 1,800 sites and about 80 million events a month on Postgres, plus one large site at 400 million events a month on ClickHouse. Write your design before you look: what a funnel is as a query over the stored events and what it costs, how far back retention can honestly see given how visitors are identified, what the optional site-supplied visitor id changes and what it costs, and what 'delete this website' and 'delete this visitor' mean in each store, aggregates included. Then tick the checkpoints you covered and add up the weights (suggested pass: 70% with every [w3] hit)

keyPoints.text: [w3] A funnel is a chain of joins on the session id: level one is every session that hit the first path or event in the range, and each later level keeps the sessions that hit the next step within the window (in minutes) after the previous step's time; each level reports a distinct count of sessions.

[w2] Cost grows with steps and filters: five steps are five joins back into the raw events for the range, and every property filter on a step adds an exists subquery into the flattened property rows, so on Postgres funnels need a bounded range and cached results, and the 400M-event site runs them on the columnar path.

[w3] Retention can only see returns inside one identity period: the report assigns each session to the cohort of its first day and joins later activity back through the same session id, and that id is re-derived whenever the salt period turns over (monthly unless configured to week or day), so a visitor coming back after the boundary is a new cohort member; with daily rotation, day-one returns are always zero.

[w3] A site-supplied id changes the derivation: the session id is then built from the site and that id with no period salt, so identified users keep one session across periods and long cohorts work for them alone; the price is a persistent personal identifier, with consent, disclosure and an erasure duty attached to it.

[w3] Deleting a website removes its events, properties, sessions, replays and revenue in one Postgres transaction, but the code never addresses ClickHouse, so on the large site the raw events, session properties and hourly rollup rows all survive; erasure there needs explicit deletes against every ClickHouse table, tracked until they complete.

[w3] 'Delete this visitor' is only as good as your ability to find them: the id is a one-way name-based UUID over a hash that includes the server secret, so no stored column leads from a person to their rows; you must recompute their ids from what they give you (address and browser for each salt period) or use their site-supplied id, and anything recorded under other inputs stays unfindable.

[w2] Aggregates are not anonymous here: the hourly rollup keeps one row per visit with the session id, browser, device and country, region and city, so erasure must reach it as well as the raw events, or the dashboard keeps describing the deleted visitor.
[w1] Any new column the features need (an erasure marker, a cohort key) has to exist in both stores, because the schemas are maintained separately.
keyPoints.quote: Forgetting this is a real trap: a column added only to Prisma won't exist for ClickHouse deployments.

questions.prompt: PRE-MORTEM — the features ship and three tickets arrive. A visitor's erasure request was confirmed, yet weeks later the large site's dashboard still shows their city; a customer's checkout funnel reports far fewer step-3 conversions on the 1st of every month than on other days; and a site that sends its own visitor id only after login sees retention for logged-in users that looks impossibly high in some weeks and impossibly low in others. What breaks, how does each show up, and what in your design prevents it?

keyPoints.text: [w3] The confirmation was untrue on ClickHouse: the delete and reset paths run only Prisma deletes, and the ClickHouse tables have no retention TTL, so the data was never going to fade in days; it stays until someone deletes it. Confirmation has to wait until the ClickHouse deletes report complete and a verification query finds nothing.

[w2] Deleting raw events does not clean the rollup: the hourly table is filled by a materialized view at insert time and is a table of its own, so an erasure job deletes from the view's target as well as from the event, property and session-property tables.

[w3] The step-3 dip is the funnel join meeting the salt boundary: a buyer who does steps one and two at 23:50 on the 31st and step three at 00:05 gets a new session id after the turn of the month, and the level join, which matches on session id within the window, drops them; report funnels within one salt period or flag windows that cross a boundary. This is the same mechanism that splits unique visitors, seen through the funnel.

[w3] Late identification splits one person in two: hits before login are named by the hashed derivation and hits after it by the site id, so the person appears as two sessions; the identified session joins a cohort on the day of login, while the anonymous one never returns, distorting both the numerator and the cohort size.

[w2] Stitching needs an explicit mapping: session properties are kept per site and session, with replacement on that key, so linking an anonymous session to a later id is a new mapping row (anonymous session to visitor id) that cohort queries join through, or the site sends its id from the first hit.

[w1] The retention report stops at day 31, close to a monthly salt period, so weekly cohorts beyond a month need the site id or must be presented as unavailable, not computed from data that cannot support them.

questions.prompt: TRADE-OFF HANDBACK — defend your feature design against the alternatives: rotating hashed visitor ids versus an opt-in site-supplied id for cohort features; hard deletes versus tombstones plus re-aggregation for erasure; answering funnels from raw events versus materializing per-step rollups; and one store for every deployment versus the split by deployment size. For each, say what you bought and what it cost.

keyPoints.text: [w3] Rotating ids keep the no-consent promise and make cohorts honest only inside one period, whose length is a deployment setting that defaults to a month; a site id unlocks month-over-month cohorts and cross-period funnels, but it is personal data, needs consent, and makes every erasure request a lookup the operator must be able to perform.

[w3] Hard deletes in a columnar store rewrite data parts asynchronously and cost real I/O, though a whole-site deletion can drop or rewrite monthly partitions; a tombstone filtered at read time confirms instantly, but the bytes still exist until a compaction removes them, which an erasure deadline must bound.

[w2] Raw-event funnels answer any step definition after the fact, at join cost; per-step rollups are fast but fix the steps in advance. The existing hourly rollup cannot stand in, because it keeps a visit's paths and event names as merged arrays with only entry and exit pages ordered, so the order and timing of steps inside a window is lost.

[w2] The split lets small self-hosts stay on Postgres and the big site scale on ClickHouse, but every funnel, cohort and erasure path is written, tested and proven twice, because the stores differ in shape, not only in dialect.
keyPoints.quote: This is why `saveEvent` has two genuinely different implementations, not just two dialects.

keyPoints.text: [w1] Keeping a deleted website as a soft-deleted row preserves recovery and references, but every analytics read must then treat it as absent, which is exactly the kind of filter that gets forgotten.
